messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 74
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Physical Therapist
  trauma_type: Refugee
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Event Recall: Talking about the event, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat, Alcohol Use: drink alcohol, Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event
  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Marta Voss is a 74-year-old European-born woman who has been married for nearly five decades and continues to work part-time as a physical therapist at a rehabilitation clinic in the mid-Atlantic city where she has lived for most of her adult life. She was referred for psychological assessment following a conversation with her primary care physician, to whom she had finally disclosed, after considerable hesitation, that she had not been sleeping well and that certain moments in her day were becoming increasingly difficult to manage.

Marta was born in the early 1950s in a country then under Soviet-aligned governance, and as a young woman in her mid-twenties she fled with her husband across a heavily militarized border during a period of acute political repression. The crossing was made at night, through a forested corridor, guided by a man neither of them fully trusted. At one point the group was halted by border guards, and there was shouting, the sound of boots on frozen ground, the acrid smell of something burning — a signal fire, she later understood, though in the moment she could not be certain. One of the guards was visibly drunk, and she could smell the alcohol on him when he leaned close to inspect her documents. She was certain, in that moment, that she would be taken. They were eventually waved through, but the hours that followed — cold, silent, disorienting — left an impression that decades of settled life in America did not fully erase.

For many years, Marta managed. She built a career, raised children, and became, by most accounts, a composed and capable woman. But in the years since her retirement began to approach and her daily structure loosened, certain things began pressing in with new insistence. The smell of alcohol — at a family dinner, at a patient's bedside when a visitor arrived — would arrest her entirely. She would find herself not in the rehabilitation gym but back in that forest, the guard's breath on her face, the documents shaking in her hands. The smell of something burning — a patient using a heating pad too long, or smoke drifting from a neighbor's yard — produced a similar arrest. She had begun, she told her therapist, to feel that she was never quite sure which moment she was in. The memories came not as recollections but as presences: she could hear the shouting, the boots, the particular cadence of commands barked in a language she had spent years trying not to think about. She saw it in images — the guard's coat, the tree line, the flashlight beam — vivid and immediate, as though no time had passed at all.

At work, she had developed the habit of positioning herself near the clinic's entrance whenever possible, scanning the waiting room each time the door opened. She told herself this was professional attentiveness, but she had come to understand, in quieter moments, that she was watching for something she could not name precisely — only that strangers approaching her in the corridor sometimes made her step back, her heart moving before her mind could intervene. She had begun keeping a small bottle of wine at home and drinking a glass, sometimes two, each evening, finding that it quieted the listening she did compulsively after dark — the listening for sounds at the door, for footsteps on the stairs that might mean someone was entering the house.

She had also begun spending long portions of her evenings in a kind of interior comparison, measuring the woman she was now against the woman she remembered being before that night — someone who, she believed, had been less watchful, less easily startled, more fully present in her own life. She had not spoken of any of this to her husband, who had made his own peace with what they had survived and did not, she felt, carry it the way she did.

What finally brought her to seek help was a moment at the clinic when a colleague's cologne — sharp, fermented — caused her to grip a treatment table and be unable to speak for nearly a minute. A younger colleague noticed. The embarrassment of that, more than the episode itself, moved her to make the call. What she most fears, she said quietly in her first session, is that this will not get better. What she most hopes is that she might, at last, be able to speak about what happened without feeling that it is still happening.
